segments.text: This kernel is the dot product. Multiply two vectors element by element, add the products, return one number. In a FIR filter that number is one output sample.
The generic version is the definition. One multiply and one add per element, and every other version in this file has to match it to within rounding.
SSE processes sixteen floats per trip. Four registers of four lanes each, multiplied pairwise, and added into four separate accumulators so the adds do not wait on each other.
After the loop, the accumulators are combined and their four lanes are added one by one. That is the horizontal reduction, and every SIMD version ends with one.
Sixteen does not divide every length, so a scalar tail loop finishes the last few elements exactly as the generic version would.
The SSE3 version is the SSE version with two operands swapped. It is a rung with nothing on it, kept so the dispatcher has an SSE3 entry.

SSE4 point 1 adds a dot product instruction. Four calls, each writing its sum into a different lane and zeros elsewhere, then combined with a bitwise or instead of an add. Elegant, and usually slower.
AVX is SSE with registers twice as wide. Eight floats per register, still sixteen per trip, so two accumulators do the work of four. Same reduction, same tail.
AVX2 with FMA is the version most modern x86 machines run. One fused multiply add does both operations with a single rounding, and the arithmetic is one line.
Eight lanes are stored and summed, then the tail loop mops up.
AVX five twelve is the same code at sixteen lanes per instruction.
On Arm, NEON keeps four accumulators and uses a multiply accumulate, then folds the lanes down in two steps. NEON version 8 swaps in a fused multiply add and a single across-vector sum.
At run time VOLK takes the highest-ranked variant this CPU supports, walking the tree from the top, unless a profile run has recorded a measured winner for this machine.
